list.listitem: The meningococcal, pneumococcal, and H. influenza type B vaccines are safe and prevent meningitis due to those pathogens.A
The initial treatment and management of meningitis in infants and children depends on early suspicion and recognition, rapid evaluation and diagnostic testing, and emergent antimicrobial therapy. A
Several validated risk scores such as the Step by Step rule and a lab-based score can predict the likelihood of invasive bacterial infection or bacterial meningitis. A
Perform lumbar puncture to obtain the cerebral spinal fluid necessary for the identification of infection-causing pathogens in order to target antimicrobial therapy. A

background.definition: Meningitis is an inflammation of the membranes enclosing the brain and spinal cord, usually caused by viruses or bacteria.

list.listitem: Overall incidence of bacterial meningitis: 8.6 per 100,000.
Streptococcus pneumoniae: 1.1 per 100,000.
Neisseria meningitidis: 0.6 per 100,000.
Group B streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae): 0.3 per 100,000.
Listeria monocytogenes: 0.2 per 100,000.
Haemophilus influenzae type b: 0.2 per 100,000.
Viral meningitis: 11 per 100,000 (highest risk in children younger than 1 year).
Bacterial meningitis in children is more common in those younger than 4 years, with a peak in infants between the ages of 3 and 8 months.

An observational study identified the prevalence of meningitis among infants presenting between ages of 8 and 60 days with a diagnosis of fever. The rate was 0.16% in preterm infants and 0.05% in term infants.
Bacteria: organisms vary by age (see ).
Viruses: 85% to 90% enterovirus (coxsackie B and echoviruses, more common in the summer and early fall), herpes simplex virus in a neonate.
Fungi: Candida species in ill, premature, and immunocompromised children and Cryptococcus neoformans.
Tuberculosis: on the rise worldwide; rare in developed countries.
Parasites.
Other aseptic meningitis causes: spirochetal infections and medications including NSAIDS and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
Organisms penetrate the subarachnoid space most often by hematogenous spread from the upper respiratory tract, and less frequently by direct spread from a connecting site or injury.
Infection-fighting antibodies poorly penetrate the blood-brain barrier.
Bacterial cell walls contain inflammatory mediators that are released with bacterial proliferation and lysis.
These mediators lead to further damage of the blood-brain barrier, cerebral edema, impaired cerebral blood flow, and neuronal injury.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Maternal primary herpes infection: herpes simplex virus

list.listitem: The H. influenzae type b vaccine is recommended by US and European guidelines and has reduced the incidence of H. influenzae type b meningitis. A
The pneumococcal vaccine is effective in reducing invasive pneumococcal infections. A
The meningococcal vaccine is effective in reducing invasive meningococcal infections.A
The H. influenzae type b vaccine has dramatically reduced the incidence of H. influenzae type b meningitis.
The meningococcal vaccine is effective in reducing invasive meningococcal infections.

In the US, the ACIP in 2020 recommended routine vaccination with a quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate vaccine (MenACWY) for adolescents aged 11 or 12 years, with a booster dose at age 16 years. They also recommend it for the following high risk groups older than 2 months: persons who have persistent complement component deficiencies; persons receiving a complement inhibitor (e.g., eculizumab or ravulizumab); persons who have anatomic or functional asplenia; persons living with HIV; scientists routinely exposed to isolates of Neisseria meningitidis; persons identified to be at increased risk because of a meningococcal disease outbreak caused by serogroups A, C, W, or Y; persons who travel to or live in areas in which meningococcal disease is hyperendemic or epidemic; unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated first-year college students living in residence halls; and military recruits.

In 2026, despite no changes in the science, meningococcal and pneumococcal vaccines were recommended by a reconstituted ACIP panel only after shared decision-making rather than routinely. This change is opposed by most major medical groups including the American Academy of Pediatrics which continues to recommend MenACWY meningococcal vaccine at 11 to 12 years with a booster at 16 years.

In Europe, a 3 dose series for infants with a booster in the 2nd year of life has been licensed (4CMenB, Bexsero). In an observational study comparing the first 3 years of the program in England with the previous 4 years found a significant reduction in the number of cases of meningococal meningitis compared to what was expected (63 vs 253, incidence rate ratio 0.25, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.36).
Subsequently a matched case-control study evaluated 4CMenB, comparing 306 case patients with 1224 controls. Vaccine was 76% effective.
The pneumococcal vaccine is effective in reducing invasive pneumococcal infections.

The routine use of intrapartum antibiotics in laboring mothers who are positive for Group B streptococcus has caused a decrease in the rate of early onset Group B streptococcus infections, including meningitis; however, there is ongoing surveillance for emerging resistance in other organisms causing meningitis in the neonate.

Meningococcal prophylaxis is recommended within 24 hours of identification of the index case for household or child-care center contacts and anyone directly exposed to the index case's oral secretions.

Options for meningococcal prophylaxis after exposure are rifampin 5 mg/kg (for those younger than 1 month) or 10 mg/kg (for those older than 1 month) orally every 12 hours for 2 days or ceftriaxone 125 mg (for those younger than 15 years) or 250 mg (for those older than 15 years) in a single intramuscular dose. For nonpregnant adults, ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally as a single dose has also been effective.
Lumbar puncture should be performed in any patient suspected of having meningitis. A
Cerebral spinal fluid is needed for identification of infection-causing pathogens in order to target antimicrobial therapy. A

C-reactive protein, latex agglutination, and polymerase chain reaction may be helpful in the management of patients pretreated with antibiotics and in patients with negative gram stains and negative cultures. B

Differential.Differential_Features: 3 to 6 months after primary tuberculosis infection, consider in chronic aseptic meningitis
Bacteremia with signs of systemic infection

list.listitem: The classic manifestations of fever, vomiting, photophobia, and severe headache or neck pain seen in adults and older children are rarely present in infants.

In infants, nonspecific symptoms include fever, hypothermia, changes in sleeping or eating habits, irritability or lethargy, vomiting, high-pitched crying more when moved than at rest, seizures, or a bulging fontanel.
Children with meningitis who are older than 2 years may complain of headache, stiff neck, and photophobia.

In one study set in an African field hospital, the presence of 1 or more of the following symptoms in children was 79% sensitive and 80% specific for meningitis: bulging fontanel, neck stiffness, cyanosis, impaired consciousness, partial seizures, and seizures outside the febrile seizure age range.

A large, well-designed study in the European primary care setting found that the physician opinion that "something is wrong" and parent impression that "illness is different from previous illnesses" were the strongest predictors of serious infection from the history. Impaired peripheral circulation, cyanosis, convulsions, meningeal irritation, and unconsciousness were key elements in the physical examination. The physician impression that "something is wrong" identified 8 of 9 children with meningitis; only in 1 in more than 3000 cases of meningitis did physician not feel that something was wrong.
Children with meningitis may have another clinical source of infection, such as otitis media, so a lumbar puncture may be warranted in children who are toxic or who have meningeal signs.

Other systemic manifestations may help differentiate between bacterial causes of meningitis. Petechial and purpuric rash suggests N. meningitidis although a rash can be present in H. influenzae type b meningitis; joint involvement, suppurative, or reactive arthritis suggests N. meningitidis or H. influenzae type b meningitis; presence of a chronically draining ear suggests S. pneumoniae.

Cerebral spinal fluid examination using lumbar puncture (LP) should include gram stain, cell count, protein, glucose, bacterial cultures with sensitivities, and additional tests as needed (eg, polymerase chain reaction for viruses, acid-fast bacillus for tuberculosis, India ink for cryptococci, and other testing suggested by the history and examination).

A nonblinded randomized trial with 1082 infants found that LP was more likely to be successful in the seated position than lying down (64% vs 58%, p = 0.03, NNT = 16) but that early versus late stylette removal had no impact on success.
Differentiation of meningitis is based on cerebral spinal fluid findings (see ).

Consider polymerase chain reaction for herpes simplex virus in a neonate, particularly those younger than 28 days, with a prenatal history of maternal genital herpes infection, lesions that appear to be caused by herpes simplex virus, or symptoms of CNS infection including seizures.

If antibiotics are given before lumbar puncture, cerebral spinal fluid findings are usually still indicative of bacterial meningitis. Cerebral spinal fluid sterilization after initiation of antibiotics is approximately 2 hours for meningococcus and 4 hours for pneumococcus.
Latex agglutination tests may be helpful when patients have been treated with antibiotics prior to lumbar puncture and the gram stain and cerebral spinal fluid cultures are negative.
Blood cultures and elevated peripheral WBC alone are not specific for the diagnosis but should be part of the diagnostic testing.
In a large series of otherwise healthy term infants who were febrile in the ED, the presence of an abnormal urinalysis did not change the likelihood of meningitis.

A systematic review found that procalcitonin levels in blood (specificity 0.97, sensitivity 0.95) and CSF (specificity 0.86, sensitivity 0.80) may be useful as a marker for bacterial meningitis; however, there were a small number of studies included and heterogenous diagnostic thresholds were used.
When clinically suspected based on imaging and/or CSF findings, obtain AFB smear, Xpert or Ultra PCR and culture from CSF. PCR is prioritized if the CSF volume is limited.

The Bacterial Meningitis Scoreis an accurate and validated decision support tool to guide clinical decision making in children with suspected bacterial meningitis in the post H. influenzae and S. pneumococcal vaccination era (see ).
The sequential "Step by Step" rule predicts the risk of invasive bacterial infection in febrile infants less than 90 days of age.

The PECARN Febrile Infant Rule has been prospectively validated and accurately predicts the likelihood of serious bacterial infection in infants younger than 60 days. Infants classified as low risk had negative urinalysis/dipstick test results, serum procalcitonin levels ≤ 0.5 ng/mL, and blood absolute neutrophil counts (ANC) ≤ 4000/mm3.

The PECARN rule was evaluated in non-ill appearing febrile infants 28 days or younger. The negative predictive value was 99.4% for invasive bacterial infections. No cases of bacterial infection were missed.

The PECARN group also derived (but has not yet validated) risk scores for febrile infants 61 to 90 days of age who were previously healthy and not critically ill. Infants with procalcitonin ≤ 0.24 ng/ml and absolute neutrophil count ≤ 10,710 cells/mm3 were low risk with 100% sensitivity in a population of 1207 infants.

For previously healthy febrile (rectal temp >= 38.0 C) infants 8 to 60 days of age, the AAP classifies them as low risk if they have ANC ≤ 5200/mm3, CRP ≤ 20 mg/L, and temperature ≤ 38.5°C. In a study of 1987 such infants, 38 had invasive bacterial infection (IBI) and none with IBI were in the low risk group.
The Meningitis Score for Emergencies estimates the likelihood that a child 1 month to 14 years of age has a bacterial cause of meningitis.

The World Health Organization Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) referral criteria for meningitis are: lethargy, unconsciousness, inability to feed, stiff neck, or seizures. These criteria are 85% sensitive and 59% specific for bacterial meningitis.

In a contemporary population of over 8000 infants, the modified Boston criteria (WBC ≥20 000 cells/mm3, UA with >10 WBC/HPF or positive urine dip result, and CSF WBC ≥10 cells/mm3) and modified Philadelphia criteria (WBC ≥15,000 cells/mm3, CSF WBC ≥8 cells/mm3, positive CSF Gram-stain result, and UA with >10 WBC/HPF or positive urine dip result) lacked accuracy.
See algorithm in for a recommended approach to treatment of infants and children outside of the neonatal period.
Empirical therapy should be based on the anticipated pathogens for a given patient's age; definitive therapy is based on the susceptibility of cultured pathogens. A
Antibiotics should be initiated as soon as possible after the diagnosis is considered likely.
Empirical therapy should be based on the anticipated pathogens for a given patient's age; definitive therapy is based on the susceptibility of cultured pathogens (see and ).

There is limited evidence regarding the appropriate duration of antibiotic therapy. One randomized trial found no difference in the rate of treatment failure between 10 and 14 days, while a cohort study found no advantage to a duration greater than 21 days.
Once a pathogen is isolated and susceptibility testing is performed, specific therapy can be tailored.

Cochrane review found that adjuvant dexamethasone reduces hearing loss and neurological sequelae in high-income countries, but does not reduce mortality. Studies do not support the use of adjuvant steroids in low-income studies.
A Cochrane review found that in patients with tuberculous meningitis, corticosteroids reduced the risk of death.

An international guideline (2026) recommended 9 to 12 months of anti-tuberculosis therapy for tuberculous meningitis. It also recommended dexamethasone 0.3 to 0.6 mg/kg/day (max 18 mg/day) or prednisone 2 mg/kg/day (max 60 mg/day) for children with tuberculous meningitis who were HIV negative. Benefit is less clear in HIV positive patients.
Intracranial pressure monitoring of meningitis patients who require mechanical ventilation has not been shown to alter mortality.
Assure adequate airway, breathing, and circulation.
Maintain adequate hydration and normal electrolyte values.

In critically ill adults with severe bacterial meningitis, therapeutic hypothermia did not improve outcomes and may lead to increased mortality. There are no trials of therapeutic hypothermia in children.
For patients with at least 1 Bacterial Meningitis Score risk factor or who are younger than 2 months, hospitalization is recommended.

For patients older than 2 months with a Bacterial Meningitis Score of 0 and who are well appearing, consider hospitalization or outpatient management. With outpatient management, consider administration of a long-acting parenteral antibiotic prior to discharge.
Other guidelines recommend hospitalization of all toxic-appearing infants younger than 28 days for cultures including blood, urine, and cerebral spinal fluid, as well as parenteral antibiotics.
For syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH), watch electrolytes, particularly sodium levels, as well as the specific gravity of the urine.
Monitor and treat seizures as necessary.

Monitor neurologic status for even subtle changes indicative of a problem, such as cranial nerve palsy, venous sinus thrombosis, cerebral spinal fluid flow obstruction, brain abscess, or cerebral infarction.
Overall mortality is less than 10% with prompt and adequate antimicrobial therapy and supportive treatment. A
Postmeningitis follow-up should include evaluation for neurologic sequelae with ongoing hearing and developmental testing. C

In aseptic meningitis, long-term cognitive development appears to be as favorable in children younger than 2 years who experience CNS complications such as complex seizures as in the children who do not experience these complications.
Prognosis depends on the patient's age, time before antibiotic initiation, causative organism and sensitivity, and patient's own inflammatory response.
Overall mortality from bacterial meningitis is 5% to 10%. In the pediatric age group, mortality is highest in neonates.
Infections caused by Group B streptococcus, gram negative enteric bacilli, and pneumococci are associated with poorer outcomes from disease then those caused by H. influenzae and meningococci.

In a large meta-analysis, the mean probabilities of sequelae after acute bacterial meningitis were: deafness, 10.5%; bilateral severe or profound deafness, 5.1%; mental retardation, 4.2%; spasticity and/or paresis, 3.5%; seizure disorder, 4.2%; and no detectable sequelae, 84%.

In a contemporary series of 62 patients with invasive H. influenzae infection in Alaska, 69% occurred in healthy children with no underlying conditions. Six children died and seven had long-term sequelae one year later.
Lumbar puncture should be repeated in any patient not responding clinically after 48 hours of appropriate antimicrobial therapy.
Lumbar puncture should be repeated in neonatal meningitis caused by gram negative bacilli to document cerebral spinal fluid sterilization and to determine the duration of therapy.
Follow up with evaluation for neurologic sequelae with ongoing hearing and developmental assessments.

feature.caption: Bacterial Meningitis Score Rule 277.
feature.feature_body: How many of the following risk factors does the patient have? Positive CSF gram stain CSF absolute neutrophil count of at least 1000 cells/ml CSF absolute neutrophil count of at least 1000 cell/ml cells/ml CSF absolute neutrophil count of at least 1000 cells/ml CSF absolute neutrophil count of at least 1000 cell/ml cells/ml CSF protein of at least 80 mg/dL Peripheral blood absolute neutrophil count of at least 10,000 cells/ml History of seizure before or at the time of presentation No risk factors: low risk for bacterial meningitis (0.1%) ≥1 risk factors: at risk for bacterial meningitis (98% sensitive, 62% specific). However, in children older than 2 months, sensitivity is 100%; in infants younger than 2 months, sensitivity is only 92%. Therefore, use this score with caution in an infant younger than 2 months.
